title: Ukraine's experiment with foreign reformers
gist: Ukraine tested three models of using foreign experts to reform post-2014 institutions: appointing foreigners to top posts and giving them advisory seats both failed, while giving international experts a decisive vote on selection commissions (as with the High Anti-Corruption Court) produced measurable results. That model now underpins EU accession conditions, but political will to keep it remains uneven.

insights.claim: Ukraine's post-2014 police reform under Georgian appointees Eka Zguladze and Khatia Dekanoidze largely failed: 5,257 officers were dismissed after vetting, but Dekanoidze said more than 90% were reinstated through the courts.
insights.so_what: Personnel purges fail when the courts and laws behind them stay unreformed, a warning for anyone pricing governance reform in transition economies.
insights.quote: Dekanoidze later claimed that more than 90 per cent had been reinstated
insights.locator: The attempt to reform the police
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Placing foreign reformers at the top of unreformed Ukrainian institutions did not produce transformation, because legal loopholes and an unreformed judiciary blocked their decisions and several foreign-born ministers resigned citing systemic resistance.
insights.so_what: Reform headlines built on star appointees are a weak signal; look at whether the enforcement chain is reformed too.
insights.quote: the reform turned out to be only as strong as the system supporting it
insights.locator: The attempt to reform the police
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Giving international experts a minority, non-decisive role on Ukrainian selection commissions produced compromised appointments, such as the first anti-corruption prosecutor (SAPO) head Nazar Kholodnytskyi, who was recorded appearing to tip off suspects and only resigned in 2020.
insights.so_what: Foreign involvement without a veto gives legitimacy cover without changing outcomes.
insights.quote: participation without the power to block a candidate could result in questionable outcomes
insights.locator: The second approach pursued by the Ukrainian
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Ukraine's State Bureau of Investigation is still not seen as fully independent of the President's Office even after a 2019 restart, and the EU's 2025 Enlargement Report asks for merit-based selection of its leaders with independent experts nominated by international partners.
insights.so_what: SBI independence is a specific gating item that could delay Ukraine's EU accession timeline.
insights.quote: This has the potential to delay Ukraine’s bid for European Union membership
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the State Bureau of Investigation
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Embedding international experts with a decisive vote in selection commissions is the model that worked in Ukraine: in the High Anti-Corruption Court selection, the Public Council of International Experts let only 7 of 49 candidates with integrity questions proceed, out of 342 applicants for 39 seats.
insights.so_what: How foreign oversight is structured, not just whether it exists, decides whether anti-corruption institutions are credible.
insights.quote: of 49 candidates whose integrity was questioned, only seven were allowed to proceed
insights.locator: The resistance to this overarching plan
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Before Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court opened, courts delivered fewer than ten high-level corruption convictions a year; by mid-2026 the HACC had delivered more than 400 verdicts, with verdicts up 41% in 2025 alone.
insights.so_what: A measurable rise in enforcement output supports the case that Ukraine's rule-of-law risk is improving.
insights.quote: By mid-2026, the HACC had delivered more than 400 verdicts. In 2025 alone, the number of verdicts grew by 41 per cent.
insights.locator: The performance data reflects this shift
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Ukraine's anti-corruption bodies NABU and SAPO had recovered UAH 11.4 billion (about £189 million) for the state as of December 2025.
insights.so_what: Asset recovery gives a concrete number for judging anti-corruption effectiveness alongside donor and reconstruction funding.
insights.quote: NABU and SAPO together had recovered UAH 11.4 billion (£189 million) for the state as of December 2025
insights.locator: The performance data reflects this shift
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Political actors in Ukraine resisted the decisive-vote model: five parliament-appointed commission members blocked approval of Oleksandr Klymenko as SAPO head for months after December 2021, until the EU made the appointment a condition of Ukraine's candidate status in July 2022.
insights.so_what: EU conditionality is the main lever forcing anti-corruption appointments through, so accession pressure is a key driver of governance quality.
insights.locator: For the selection of the next head of SAPO
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Public trust in Ukraine's courts recovers slowly: 70% distrusted the HACC in 2020, and distrust of the general court system fell from 77.5% then to 66% in November 2025, while 57% of anti-corruption experts in a 2025-26 OSCE-backed survey rated the HACC effective.
insights.so_what: Expert confidence is running ahead of public trust, so institutional credibility gains may take years to show up in the polls.
insights.locator: Public trust did not come immediately
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Ukraine's revised draft Anti-Corruption Strategy for 2026-30 keeps a decisive vote for international experts in selecting the SBI head but downgrades them to 'temporary involvement' for the High Council of Justice, a sign of uneven political will.
insights.so_what: Rolling back foreign veto rights is an early warning of reform backsliding worth tracking in the accession process.
insights.quote: it no longer guarantees them one in selecting members of the High Council of Justice, providing only for their ‘temporary involvement’
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova

insights.claim: Foreign decision-making power in Ukrainian vetting should be temporary; the real test is whether Ukraine builds checks and balances credible enough not to need outside experts.
insights.so_what: Investors should judge Ukraine's governance by self-sustaining institutions, not by external scaffolding that could be withdrawn.
insights.quote: This should not, however, be considered a permanent arrangement.
insights.speaker: Kseniya Sotnikova
